what_it_measures: Share of frame area sitting at or above OKLCH chroma 0.19, which is the threshold both chroma-budget gates use
how_it_was_measured: Every pixel of a 160px-long-edge copy through plan_palette.rgb_to_oklab, chroma as hypot(a, b), then the share at or above 0.19
distribution: 190 of 244 frames (77.9%) carry no loud pixel at all. 10 (4.1%) exceed 3 percent. One (0.4%) exceeds the 20 percent gate, and it is a single red-dress frame at 40.8 percent
claim_it_grades: Combined share of colours at C >= 0.19 is <= 20 percent of the visible area
where_that_claim_lives: data/colour-gates.csv, gate chroma-budget-by-surface-share; the number is CHROMA_SHARE_MAX in scripts/plan_palette.py
what_changes: 20 percent stays the fail line for a flat layout, where a full-bleed brand panel is a legitimate surface. For a photograph or a photo-derived render the working line is 3 percent: 96 percent of this set sits under it, and a gate at 20 percent passes a frame roughly seventy-seven times louder than the p90 of professional practice, so on photographic output it is not doing any work
what_this_cannot_tell_you: A photograph is not a palette. Skin, fabric and daylight are physically low-chroma in sRGB, so some of this result is what a camera can record rather than what an art director chose. It does not license lowering the layout threshold to 3 percent

what_it_measures: How many 30-degree hue families each hold at least 5 percent of frame area at C >= 0.19 - the photograph's analogue of counting loud swatches in a palette
how_it_was_measured: Loud pixels bucketed into the twelve hue families, then families counted only where their loud area reaches 5 percent of the frame
distribution: 238 of 244 frames carry zero loud families, 6 carry exactly one, none carries two
claim_it_grades: At most 1 colour at or above C 0.19
where_that_claim_lives: data/colour-gates.csv, gate chroma-budget-by-count; the number is CHROMA_BUDGET_LOUD_MAX in scripts/plan_palette.py
what_changes: Nothing. The ceiling of one is never broken here, but it is never approached either: only 7 frames of 244 (2.9%) reach C 0.19 even at their 95th-percentile pixel. A sample that rarely gets near a limit cannot confirm it, so the gate keeps its house-rule grade instead of being promoted on evidence that only looks like support
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Whether two loud colours would actually fail. Nothing in this set attempts it, so the gate is a convention that has not been contradicted rather than one that has been tested

what_it_measures: The chroma of the 95th-percentile pixel: how loud a professional frame gets at its loudest
how_it_was_measured: Pixel chroma in OKLCH, weighted by pixel count, read at the 95th and 50th percentiles
measured: p95 pixel: p10 0.0338, median 0.0713, p90 0.1577, max 0.2149. Median pixel: median 0.0228
distribution: The median frame peaks at 38 percent of the loud threshold. 7 of 244 (2.9%) reach it
claim_it_grades: None. The skill had a threshold for loud and no measurement of what loud looks like in delivered work
where_that_claim_lives: Nowhere, which is the finding. C 0.19 was adopted as a limit with no reference point on the other side of it
what_changes: Gives the loud threshold the scale it never had. C 0.19 is not a line professional photography brushes against; it is about 2.7 times the peak chroma of a median frame. A palette built to sit just under the gate is still far louder than the reference set
what_this_cannot_tell_you: How the chroma was arrived at. A muted grade over a saturated scene and a muted scene shot straight measure identically

what_it_measures: Which aspect ratio the frame was actually delivered at, bucketed to the nearest of the seven feed ratios in frame-ratios.csv
how_it_was_measured: Width over height from the file header, no decoding, matched to the nearest listed ratio
measured: 4:5 is the default at 173 of 244 frames (70.9%)
claim_it_grades: 1:1 belongs to marketplace tiles, ad units, carousels and the legacy IG feed
what_changes: Legacy now has a number behind it: three frames in 244. A run that offers 1:1 for a person-led feed post is offering the ratio a professional feed has abandoned. 2:3 appeared zero times, which is the same finding one step stronger
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Whether 1:1 still earns the rest of its native_home cell. Marketplace tiles and ad units are where frame-ratios.csv also places it, and this set contains none of either

what_it_measures: Whether the default ratio is a house style or a function of what the account is for
how_it_was_measured: The same ratio buckets, held separately per account, with the group and brand account distinguished from the four personal ones
measured: The group and brand account runs 9:16 in 38 of 44 frames. All four personal accounts default to 4:5, in 34 to 50 of 50
claim_it_grades: 4:5 is the Meta feed ratio, the most feed area available without being a Story
what_changes: Ratio follows register, not taste. A brand or group account is vertical-video-first and a person account is 4:5-first, so a run cannot answer what ratio before it has answered who is posting. The two are separate questions and the skill was treating them as one
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Why. A brand account posts more stage and performance footage, which is natively 9:16, so the ratio may be following the source material rather than a channel decision

what_it_measures: How many 30-degree hue families each carry at least 5 percent of the frame, counting only pixels that make a hue decision at all
how_it_was_measured: Pixels above HSV saturation 0.15 bucketed into twelve families; families holding under 5 percent of the frame counted as accents, not palette members
distribution: 0 families in 7 frames, 1 in 44, 2 in 90, 3 in 68, 4 in 26, 5 in 5, 6 in 3, 7 in 1. 141 of 244 (57.8%) at two or fewer, 209 (85.7%) at three or fewer
where_that_claim_lives: data/reference-observations.csv, palette_structure column, rows winter-mirror-doll and karina-prada-collage - each an observation of one post
what_changes: Two is the median, so it is the right target, but it is not the rule: 42 percent of professional frames carry three or more families. State it as a ceiling of three with a target of two, so a run stops deleting a third hue the reference set treats as normal
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Which family is skin. Orange is both the skin family and a real wardrobe and set colour, so a frame counted at two may be one deliberate hue plus skin, or two deliberate hues on a pale subject

what_it_measures: Share of the frame carrying no hue decision - a value decision instead
how_it_was_measured: Pixels below HSV saturation 0.15, as a share of the frame
distribution: Per-account medians run 0.318 (imwinter) to 0.481 (goyounjung). Every account sits between a third and a half
claim_it_grades: Background dressing should locate the photo without competing - stated as prose, with no share attached
what_changes: Puts a number on not competing, which was the whole of the claim and none of the instruction: about 40 percent of a professional frame is doing no colour work at all. A generated frame where every surface carries a hue is not a stylistic variant of this, it is a different structure
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Where the neutral area sits. A neutral wall behind the subject and a neutral outfit against a coloured wall give the same share and read nothing alike

what_it_measures: How much of the tonal range the frame actually uses, as the 95th percentile of value minus the 5th
how_it_was_measured: HSV value per pixel, weighted by pixel count. p95 minus p5 rather than max minus min, so one blown specular highlight does not decide the contrast of a photograph
distribution: Per-account medians 0.753 to 0.804 - the tightest agreement of any axis here
claim_it_grades: None. The skill asks for light quality and direction and never for a tonal range
where_that_claim_lives: Nowhere. The light references describe sources and modifiers, not the histogram they produce
what_changes: A professional frame uses close to the whole value range, and every account agrees within five points. A flat mid-tone render - which is the default an unprompted model produces - is measurably not this look, so asking for a black point and a real highlight is asking for the thing the reference set has
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Whether the range came from the lighting or the grade. Both land in the same histogram

what_it_measures: How much of the frame sits in the deep end and the bright end - area below value 0.25 and above 0.75
how_it_was_measured: Pixel counts in each band as a share of the frame
distribution: Shadow p10 0.050, p90 0.548. Highlight p10 0.061, p90 0.643. Near-symmetric at the median and wide at both tails
claim_it_grades: None. Shadow is discussed as a quality and a direction, never as an area budget
where_that_claim_lives: Nowhere. The reference observations describe shadow placement, for example almost no shadow under the jaw, without a share
what_changes: Roughly a fifth of the frame at each end, and the two ends are balanced. Shadow is not something professional work minimises: the median frame gives a fifth of its area to it, which contradicts the bright-and-even default a soft-light brief tends to produce
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Whether the shadow is on the subject or the set. A dark background and a shadowed face give the same share and are opposite decisions

what_it_measures: Whether the frame leans warm or cool, as warm pixels minus cool pixels over all pixels carrying a hue
how_it_was_measured: Warm as hue under 75 or over 315 degrees, cool as 165 to 285, difference divided by the coloured pixel count. Plus 1 is entirely warm, minus 1 entirely cool
distribution: Per account: for_everyoung10 +0.828, katarinabluu +0.658, imwinter +0.540, aespa_official +0.379, goyounjung +0.285. Every account is warm at the median; the difference is how warm
claim_it_grades: None. Colour temperature appears in lighting recipes as a Kelvin value, never as a frame-level balance
where_that_claim_lives: Nowhere. data/palettes.csv carries hues and the light recipes carry temperatures, and no row states which way a frame should lean
what_changes: Warm is the default and cool is the deliberate exception, not a free choice between two equals. A brief asking for cool and editorial is asking for the minority frame and should be told so, because a run that picks cool by accident has picked the p10 of professional practice
what_this_cannot_tell_you: How much of the warmth is skin. Skin fills a large share of every frame here, so a portrait set cannot separate a warm grade from a warm subject

what_it_measures: Which single hue family holds the most coloured area in the frame
how_it_was_measured: The largest of the twelve family buckets, or neutral where no pixel cleared the saturation floor
measured: Orange leads 113 of 244 frames (46.3%). The blue side - azure 40 plus blue 25 - leads 65 (26.6%)
distribution: orange 113, azure 40, red 34, blue 25, yellow 7, rose 5, spring-green 5, yellow-green 5, neutral 4, cyan 3, violet 2, green 1
claim_it_grades: None. The palette tables name harmony structures without saying which hue tends to lead a photograph
where_that_claim_lives: Nowhere. The colour-harmony dossier gives the structures, not the population
what_changes: The set is a warm subject against a cool surround: orange leads nearly half the frames, the blue side leads a quarter, and the remaining ten families share 13 percent. Green leads once in 244, so a green-dominant frame is not a safe default dressed up as a fresh one
what_this_cannot_tell_you: Whether the pattern is a choice or a location. Indoor tungsten and outdoor blue hour both produce a warm subject on a cool ground
